What is genuinely missing is any poll or host-pushed update, so a change made outside the editor - the host CLI's own setLan (packages/host/src/cli/hosting.ts:29), or a host restart - is not observed until the page is reloaded or the control is pressed in-editor, and the live indicator renders a stale claim meanwhile. OWNER: Task 4's status bar owns the live indicator (its brief names PublishIndicator reading this store), so the fix belongs there if it is judged worth making; the alternative is to accept that the editor is the only in-session writer and close this as by-design. NOT FIXED in Task 3 because polling policy is the indicator's concern, not the header control's. SEVERITY: low - needs an external writer against the same host while the editor is open to be reachable at all.

title: Base UI's popover cannot be closed under jsdom, so the close half of any popover contract is browser-only
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 3's fix round while restoring the address case in src/web/packages/editor/src/editor-shell/publish-control.dom.test.tsx. Re-adding an assertion that the surface closes throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name') from inside Base UI's own close path, with no reachable stack. MEASURED: jsdom only - the same close IS proved in tests/e2e/publish-header.spec.ts, where a real browser hides the surface on a second press on the control. CONSEQUENCE: a dom test in this repo can assert that a popover OPENS but not that it CLOSES, so the close half of a popover contract is browser-only; whoever writes that assertion next and sees it throw will reasonably conclude the component is broken, when the harness is. The case was left asserting the open half, and the close half lives in the browser spec. OWNER/FIX: unassigned - a jsdom shim for whatever property Base UI reads off the close event would move it, but keeping close-path assertions in e2e is the honest fix until then. SEVERITY: low - a test-harness limitation with no user-visible effect.

title: No Playwright config sets outputDir, so concurrent runs share test-results and delete each other's traces, reporting false failures
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 3's fix round (its Discovered, not fixed item 6); mechanism CONFIRMED by the controller, measurement by the implementer. All five configs - playwright.config.ts, playwright.display.config.ts, playwright.glass-shapes.config.ts, playwright.parity.config.ts and playwright.rebuild.config.ts - omit outputDir, so every run writes into the same default test-results/ root and its .playwright-artifacts-N directories. Running two configs at once therefore makes the first to finish clean up the other's artifacts, and the survivor reports browserContext.close: ENOENT ... .trace as TEST FAILURES. MEASURED: playwright.rebuild.config.ts reported 2 failed / 7 passed under a concurrent display run and 9 passed / 0 failed alone. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS TASK: it is a false-red generator, so a browser run on this box is not a measurement while another run is in flight - this is the mechanism under the 'a single sample of a flaky spec is not a measurement' rule AGENTS.md already carries, and it means running two configs in parallel to save wall-clock buys phantom failures instead. OWNER/FIX: unassigned - giving each config a distinct outputDir (e.g. outputDir: 'test-results/rebuild') is the obvious fix and is a config change rather than a task. SEVERITY: medium - no product effect, but it corrupts the evidence the verification process rests on.

title: The status strip's background flattens two tones the mockup draws differently
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 4's task review. The checked reference paints a background on the status strip at docs/design/mockups/editor-shell.html:226 whose VALUE is #0e1217 - the rail's tone - while the implementation uses var(--panel) (editor-shell.css:485), which is the header's --shell-surface tone. So the mockup draws the header lighter than the strip and the implementation makes them the same tone; the implementer's report claimed the strip 'matches the mockup', which is true of the presence of a background and false of its value. RULED defensible and kept: bible section 4 forbids the hex and there is no darker token in the palette to match #0e1217, so var(--panel) is the only on-scale choice available today. The difference is therefore a real divergence from the checked reference rather than a bug, and it needs listing rather than fixing. OWNER: Task 10's difference list (plan 2 phase 3) is the natural home - it exists to enumerate exactly this kind of gap between the design language and the implementation. SEVERITY: low - one tone where the mockup has two; visible only side by side.

title: The document's name-else-id reading is spelled in three places in editor-main.ts
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 5's implementer and carried in its commit as a Discovered, not fixed trailer. The rule 'the document's name, else its id' now appears at editor-main.ts:271 and :387 (the status line) and at :294 (the bridge's projection of EditorShellSnapshot.documentName added by Task 5), so a change to how an unnamed theme is identified must be made in all three or they will disagree about what the document is called. The implementer named the cause but did not unify them, on the grounds that doing so reaches the status line's own wording, which no test pins. OWNER: unassigned - the natural fix is a single exported helper that both the status line and the bridge projection call, which is also what 'one owner per concept' asks for. SEVERITY: low today - the three spellings are identical, so nothing disagrees yet; the risk is a future edit that changes one. NOTE: this is the duplicate-reading class the same plan's Task 2 addressed for object-action eligibility with objectActionsFor(gate). UPDATE 2026-10-09 after plan 2 Task 5 fix round 1 (cf82c14f): the bridge projection no longer spells the rule - Task 5 moved it into a testable seam (bridge.ts input documentIdentity?: () => {name, id}, with the fallback taken there), so editor-main.ts:294 now hands over raw facts. That leaves the rule spelled at :271 and :387 (the status line) versus the bridge, and the divergence is now OBSERVABLE rather than theoretical: for a schema-valid theme whose metadata.name is empty, the identity chip shows the id while the status line still writes a blank "Opened ". The implementer filed that as a Discovered, not fixed trailer rather than changing the status line wording, which is a behaviour change outside Task 5 scope. This strengthens the case for the single exported helper: the two spellings have already drifted once.

title: The identity chip differs from the mockup in three ways Task 10 must list as deliberate
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 5's task review, comparing the landed chip against the checked reference at docs/design/mockups/editor-shell.html:178-184. The mockup draws (a) a 1px separator between the theme name and the edited state, (b) the WORD 'edited' in --muted, and (c) the name at font-weight 500. The implementation draws no separator, uses uiCopy.saveState.unsaved ('Unsaved changes') in the warn role, and leaves the name at weight 400. All three are defensible rather than wrong: reusing the status bar's exact word is the plan's stated single-source guarantee for save state ('two save states that disagree' is the failure mode the plan names), and bible section 7.5 names only 'record dot, theme name, edited state' without prescribing the separator or the word. The point of this row is that Task 10's difference list must record each as a deliberate choice rather than let the parity capture appear to 'discover' them. OWNER: Task 10 (plan 2 phase 3). SEVERITY: low - no user-visible defect; a documentation obligation.

title: The bridge republishes the whole shell snapshot on every document change, so menus, dock and display switch re-render per edit
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 5 (the implementer raised it against itself) and judged by its task review. To make a rename reach the new identity chip, bridge.ts:145 subscribes input.session.subscribeDocumentChange(notify) unconditionally. A rename moves no Fabric object, so no canvas event fires for it - but subscribeDocumentChange fires on far more than renames: editor-session.ts:224 (#announceChange) is called from editor:edit-committed, object:added/removed (:268-273), every envelope write (#writeEnvelope, :1010) and saves (:725, :817). So the whole EditorShellSnapshot republishes, and the menus, dock and display switch re-render on committed edits, token/binding/metadata edits and saves - not only on a rename. RULED acceptable as landed, not a defect: re-renders are idempotent, no correctness is lost, and the review judged it not a 'behaviour change' under the plan's Global Constraint (same fields, gates, refusals, markers). It is avoidable in roughly three lines - the bridge could cache the pulled name and call notify() only when it differs, since only documentName needs this signal (selectedCount/locked/activeKind already ride the canvas events) - without adding any session API. The implementer's claim that 'the session exposes no name-only signal' is literally true but half the story. OWNER: unassigned; the review's recommendation was to keep it and narrow only if a later task measures a cost. SEVERITY: low - re-render churn, no correctness loss.

title: The theme document schema gives metadata.name no minLength, so an empty name validates
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 5's task review and CONFIRMED by the controller against the schema. schema/theme-document.schema.json defines the theme's name as $defs/metadata/properties/name = {type: string, maxLength: 200} - there is NO minLength, so an imported or hand-edited envelope carrying metadata.name: "" is schema-valid. That reaches the identity chip as an empty name: editor-main.ts:294 reads metadata?.name ?? envelope.id, and ?? falls back only on null/undefined, so "" passes through and DocumentIdentity (which hides only on undefined) renders a nameless frame - the bible section 9 failure its own comment promises cannot happen. The code side was fixed in Task 5's fix round by switching to ||; THIS row is the schema side, filed rather than fixed because adding minLength: 1 would start rejecting documents that validate today, which is a compatibility decision rather than a bug fix. Evidence it is an oversight rather than a decision: the sibling $defs/fontAssetReference/properties/license/name and the palette and typePreset group names all carry minLength: 1, and the theme's own top-level name is the one that does not. OWNER: unassigned - whoever owns document validation; the decision is whether a nameless theme is legal at all. SEVERITY: low once the read site is defensive - no data is lost, and the worst case is a chip showing an id instead of a name.

title: The shell ships two competing cluster treatments, and the glass one sits off the elevation ladder in both directions
detail: FOUND BY the controller while ruling on plan 2 Task 6's cluster surface, and then MEASURED before filing rather than filed from the ruling. The product has two floating-cluster treatments. (1) The identity chip states bible section 7.5 literally: --panel at ~95%, blur(6px), elevation 1. (2) The dock (canvas-dock.tsx:126) and the view cluster (display-switch.tsx:104) carry .editor-glass (editor-shell.css:375-400), whose base is box-shadow: none - section 3's LEVEL 0, flat - and whose five non-editorial palettes override with a gradient background, two inset highlights, 0 18px 40px #0000004a and backdrop-filter: blur(10px) saturate(135%). Against the bible that is off the ladder twice over: 0 18px 40px is section 3's LEVEL 2 (overlay) value, not the LEVEL 1 (0 8px 20px #00000059) that section 3 assigns to floating clusters over the canvas, and blur is 10px where section 3 says clusters blur their backdrop at blur(6px). Section 7.5 independently calls a cluster --panel at ~95% with backdrop blur, 1px --edge, elevation 1. So in five palettes a cluster renders at overlay elevation and in editorial it renders at no elevation at all. Worth recording precisely: the bible contains NO per-palette glass rule - section 4 says only that colour is a runtime palette of six - so 'editorial is flat and the other five are glass' is an IMPLEMENTATION choice pinned by shell-appearance.spec.ts from the earlier authoring work, not an instruction that outranks section 7.5. That matters because the tempting resolution (match the chip) reddens that spec for all six palettes, which is why Task 6 kept the glass and filed this instead. OWNER: first a design-language decision - which of the two treatments is the product's, whether the ladder's level 1 or the glass palette's overlay value wins, and what editorial does about elevation when it is deliberately flat - and then whoever owns the two surfaces. Task 10's difference list inherits it. SEVERITY: medium - nothing fails and nothing is unreachable, but two settled-looking treatments disagree in the same window and the ladder has no answer for editorial. AMENDED BY PLAN 7 TASK 5 (2026-10-11), which moved the treatment boundary: `.editor-glass` is now the CHROME default (`background: var(--panel)`, no shadow, no blur) and the two clusters opt into the glass by name (`.editor-shell-dock.editor-glass`, `.editor-shell-zoom.editor-glass`), so this row's citation of `editor-shell.css` line numbers and of a base that is `box-shadow: none` with five per-palette overrides is a stale landmark rather than a description of the file. THE FINDING IS UNCHANGED and so is the treatment this row measures: the dock and the view cluster still paint a gradient, two inset highlights, `0 18px 40px #0000004a` and `backdrop-filter: blur(10px) saturate(135%)`, and Task 5 gave `editorial`'s two clusters the same treatment, so the off-ladder cluster surface now reaches all six palettes where it reached five. Task 5 did not absorb this row: the elevation-2 shadow and the 10px blur against section 3's elevation 1 and `blur(6px)` are untouched, and the identity chip's competing treatment is untouched too.

title: The identity chip has no rule for what happens once the name is fully truncated: the fixed edited marker overflows and is clipped mid-word
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 6's completion round, from the collision assertion the controller required. At 640x360 CSS px - which is 1280x720 at the 200% browser zoom section 7.7 requires be checked - .editor-shell-identity's min-width: 0 let the chip shrink below the floor its non-shrinkable children set, so the trailing "Unsaved changes" painted from x=399 to x=483.6 while the chip's own box ended at 465 and the view cluster began at 473: a 10.6px overlap, with elementFromPoint answering SPAN where it should answer CANVAS. A comparison of the chip's BOX could never see it, which is why the assertion compares painted geometry and a point between the corners. Fixed in Task 6 with one declaration, overflow: hidden on .editor-shell-identity (editor-shell.css:1639), and that fix stands - it is containment, not surface, and R3's "do not touch the chip" ruling was about the panel/glass/elevation treatment. WHAT THIS ROW ACTUALLY IS, corrected after reading the chip's own rules rather than filing the round's framing: it is NOT that the wrong element is degraded. .editor-shell-identity-name is min-width: 0, overflow: hidden, text-overflow: ellipsis, so the name IS the only child that can shrink and it ellipsises first; the dot and the edited marker are both flex: none. So at 640x360 the name has already been truncated to nothing and the fixed marker still overflows by 10.6px - the arithmetic matches the measurement, since the chip's floor is its padding plus the 7px dot plus two gaps plus a fixed "Unsaved changes" that cannot shrink. The gap in the design language is therefore the state PAST a fully truncated name: section 7.7 licenses truncating identity's name, and says nothing about what the chip should do once the name is gone and a fixed part still does not fit. The landed behaviour is a mid-word clip with no ellipsis, which is the one presentation section 7.7 explicitly reserves for refusals and numeric edits. A future owner should NOT "make the name ellipsise instead" - it already does. The open choices are dropping or shortening the edited marker at compact widths, allowing it to wrap, or accepting the clip and saying so. OWNER: the identity chip's presentation, or Task 10's difference list; adjacent to but distinct from vg-219, which lists the chip's three mockup differences. SEVERITY: low - cosmetic, at one breakpoint, with no data, reachability or focus lost.

title: Four glyph-button hover rules wash the background where section 5 rule 6 requires an acquired --muted border
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 6's task review (low severity) and SCOPED BY MEASUREMENT by the controller before filing, so the row names a real set instead of an impression. UPDATED when Task 7 landed: the dock's instance is fixed, so the set is THREE, not four. Bible section 5 rule 6 is explicit: hover raises --edge to --muted, and on a glyph-only control with no resting border 'it is the border it acquires on hover. Nothing moves, nothing scales.' editor-shell.css carries 12 :hover rules, six of which set a background. THREE are glyph-only buttons that still hover with a wash where rule 6 prescribes the acquired border: .editor-shell-rail button:hover (:801), .editor-shell-dialog > button:hover (:1119), .vigilia-layer-row button:hover (:1400). Two instances have since been fixed and are recorded here as the pattern the remaining three want. .editor-shell-view-step:hover was introduced by Task 6 and fixed in that task's own fix round (resting border 1px transparent, hover border-color: --muted, box-sizing: border-box declared on the rule so acquiring the border moves nothing). .editor-shell-dock button:hover was fixed by Task 7 the same way (editor-shell.css:847-849), which is the ruling applied consistently: the task that owns a surface fixes that surface's own rule, and a closed task's surface is left for the sweep. EXPLICITLY NOT PART OF THIS SET, and the row should not grow to include them: the menu item and menuitemradio hovers (:621, :623) and the menubar buttons (:574) are list-row and menu affordances, which are not in section 5's closed control vocabulary at all; .editor-shell-palette:hover (:682) is a swatch well, which already carries a resting border, so rule 6's second clause does not reach it. IMPORTANT FOR WHOEVER TAKES THIS: Task 8's ratchet CANNOT catch it. That guard reads hex literals and off-scale px values and is blind to a semantic rule, so this sweep needs its own owner and its own check rather than being assumed into the ratchet's coverage. OWNER: unassigned; Task 8 is the nearest home by subject but does not cover it by mechanism. SEVERITY: low - a hover affordance that differs from the prescribed one on three controls; nothing breaks, nothing is unreachable, and the deviation is consistent with itself today.

title: The zoom readout opens a list without section 5's well-and-chevron vocabulary
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 6's task review (informational) and RULED to stand by the controller rather than treated as a nit. Bible section 5 states its control vocabulary is CLOSED - 'A control is one of these, or it is not a control' - and the entry for a control that opens a list is 'Well with chevron: a well, plus a small chevron in --faint - opens a list'. The view cluster's readout (.editor-shell-view-readout, editor-shell.css) DOES open a list: it is the display chooser's trigger, and the menu behind it holds Fit, the six lenses in their two orientation groups, zoom-to-selection and actual size. It renders as a bare percentage - min-width 56px, tabular-nums, transparent background, no well, no chevron. The tension is real in both directions, which is why it is filed rather than changed: the readout is genuinely ALSO a readout, and the closed vocabulary has no entry for a control that is a value display and a trigger at once, so the honest fix might be a design-language amendment adding that entry rather than a UI change. Deliberately not changed in Task 6 for a second reason: the readout must stay the chooser's trigger, because editor-display.spec.ts's chooseDisplay() helper clicks exactly that element and then picks a menuitemradio. OWNER: Task 10's difference list, with docs/design/mockups/ as the reference for how the display chooser should present. SEVERITY: low - every choice stays one gesture away and nothing is unreachable; this is about how the trigger is presented, not about what it can do.

title: Delete is marked destructive in the dock only, from a second owner declared inside the dock
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 7's task review, which judged it an OWNER VIOLATION rather than acceptable per-surface emphasis at LOW severity. canvas-dock.tsx:20 declares DESTRUCTIVE_ACTIONS = new Set(["delete"]), which re-decides inside the dock a fact about the registry entry (object-actions.ts:195, in the module whose own comment at :100 reads 'One owner for object actions: what each is, when it applies, how it runs'). The same registry is rendered by two other surfaces - the layer panel's footer and the canvas context menu - and NEITHER marks Delete as destructive (grep for --hot or 'destructive' across both files returns nothing), so one concept, 'this action destroys', is now expressed on one of the three surfaces that render it. The author-visible consequence: Delete is --hot in the dock and ordinary in the layer footer and the context menu, which reads as the dock warning about something the other two do not. Bible section 4 places 'destructive' on the action, so the owner is the registry entry: add a destructive flag there, let one marker be shared by all three surfaces, and delete the dock's set. Deliberately NOT fixed in Task 7 even though the mark itself came from that task's brief: object-actions.ts is outside its file set, and un-marking the dock to match the two older surfaces would trade a correct new surface for consistency with incorrect ones - the same line Task 6 drew when it fixed its own hover rule and left the rail's. It breaks nothing today: the added data-vigilia-destructive attribute is additive and leaves both equality selectors (editor.spec.ts:3877, snapping.spec.ts:581) and every aria-label untouched, which the review verified from source. OWNER: the object-action registry. SEVERITY: low.

title: The rail's slot is a 34px icon-only control, outside section 5's 26-30px icon button
detail: FOUND BY the controller while correcting a stale STATUS claim about who owned the value, and MEASURED before filing. editor-shell.css:789-790 sets the rail slot's width and height to 34px, and rail.tsx:33 documents it as 'a 34px icon-only control whose one word is both its tooltip and ...'. Bible section 5 states its control vocabulary is CLOSED - 'A control is one of these, or it is not a control' - and its icon button is 'a 26-30px square at --radius-md, glyph only'. A 34px glyph-only control is therefore either an icon button outside the range the bible states for it, or a control the closed vocabulary does not contain. NOTHING OWNS THE DECISION, which is the part worth recording: the shell plan never mentions 34; scripts/design-tokens.gated.json's biblePx array is [3, 11, 14, 26, 30, 32, 36, 46, 246, 276, 999, 1.6, 1.7, 1.8] and contains no 34; and the value lives in editor-shell.css, which is deliberately UNGATED - Task 8 records that file's hex count as a before-state for plan 3 rather than adding it to the guard - so the guard never sees it. rail.tsx IS a gated file, but it carries the 34 only inside a comment, which the guard does not read. So the one mechanism that could have caught this is blind to it twice over. Same family as vg-202 (a well's horizontal padding at 6px where section 3's table assigns 4px): a value off the bible's own table that no gate watches. OWNER: whoever owns the rail's control size - either the rail moves into 26-30px, or biblePx gains 34 and section 5 gains the entry the slot needs. SEVERITY: low, and note the direction of the risk: a target larger than the bible's range is safer than one smaller, so this is a conformance gap rather than an accessibility defect.

title: The gated list's dom-test membership is two of fifteen: which of a converted surface's tests the ratchet covers is whichever task happened to add it
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 8's task review as an observation rather than a defect, and deliberately left unfixed there — the right scope for a measurement task, since its union rule is 'each task's additions' and that rule holds. The list has 23 entries of which exactly TWO are dom test files, display-switch.dom.test.tsx and pane.dom.test.tsx, while packages/editor/src/editor-shell/ holds fifteen .dom.test.tsx files. The reviewer's own wording: 'the dom.test membership rule is genuinely inconsistent, but the report declares it inherited and out of scope.' The sharpest case is a single task: Task 2 CREATED pane.dom.test.tsx, which is gated, and MODIFIED layer-panel.dom.test.tsx (65.8 kB), which is not — and Task 8 has since gated layer-panel.tsx itself, so that surface's component is covered while the test beside it is not, and its sibling's test is. Why this is worth a row rather than a shrug: a ratchet's value is that its coverage can be trusted to mean something uniform, and today it means 'the files their own tasks chose to name'. A reader cannot tell from the list whether a missing dom test was a decision or an omission, which is the same failure mode as a vacuous gate. NOT FIXED IN TASK 8 because closing it requires choosing a rule first, and the choice is the guard owner's to make once: either every converted surface's dom test joins (which would add layer-panel.dom.test.tsx, canvas-dock.dom.test.tsx, document-identity.dom.test.tsx, publish-indicator.dom.test.tsx, publish-control.dom.test.tsx, rail.dom.test.tsx, save-state.dom.test.tsx and shell-layout.dom.test.tsx — Task 8's report measures all of them clean, so the additions cannot fail the guard), or none does (which removes the two current members and changes what plan 1's list has meant since it landed). Task 8's brief scopes this out explicitly, so it is a decision rather than an oversight. OWNER: whoever owns scripts/design-tokens.gated.json. SEVERITY: low — no value goes unchecked today; the finding is about what the list guarantees, not about a violation it misses.

title: The visual-evidence README claims every capture uses `?static=1` and a controlled clock, which is false for the editor's captures
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 9's implementer while doing the parity capture, and REPORTED rather than obeyed: the brief it worked from carried the same sentence forward and told it to use `?static=1` and the controlled clock, and the implementer checked, found the editor has neither, used the harness the two existing editor captures use, and flagged the instruction as stale. MEASURED before filing, because 'the editor has no static mode' is the kind of claim that is easy to make and cheap to check. docs/evidence/screenshots/README.md:14-15 states, as a rule for every capture: 'Captures use `?static=1` and a controlled clock.' Neither half holds for the editor. (1) The editor reads exactly ONE query parameter — packages/editor/src/editor-main.ts:383 is bootTheme(window.location.search, libraryClient), which is `?theme`. There is no `static` branch anywhere in the editor bundle. (2) Every `?static=1` in the browser suite is against the HOST/PLAYER: tests/e2e/clip-parity.spec.ts:535, display-fabric.spec.ts:757, host-bleed.spec.ts:35 and :64, all `page.goto(`${HOST}/...`)`; and tests/e2e/canvas-probe.ts:201, which appends the parameter for the player probes, is imported by exactly three specs — display-fabric.spec.ts, host-player.spec.ts, player-chrome.spec.ts — none of them an editor spec. (3) No editor capture pins a clock: the shared capture helper tests/e2e/editor-canvas.ts contains no setFixedTime or setSystemTime, and neither editor.spec.ts's captures nor design-language.spec.ts's pin one. WHY THIS IS WORTH A ROW RATHER THAN A SHRUG: the README is the instructions a capture author follows, and this sentence sent one looking for a static mode and a pinned clock the editor has never had. It cost this task a rebuild-and-check cycle and a paragraph of report, and a less careful implementer would have 'fixed' it by pausing Date in a spec, which would have changed the capture's evidence rather than its accuracy. It is the same failure shape as a vacuous gate: an instruction that reads as authoritative, cannot be satisfied, and is not checked by anything. NOTE THE EDITOR CAPTURES ARE TIME-DEPENDENT BY DESIGN — the starter clock and the live chart values are real — which is why the correct replacement is not 'the editor also gets a fixed clock' but a sentence that says which captures the rule is about. The README ALREADY CONTAINS the narrower truth elsewhere: its `## Settings page` table names `desktop-host` and `publish` projects for the captures that drive the host. NOT FIXED IN TASK 9 because its brief scopes README changes to registering the new action, and because the right replacement sentence is a decision — the blanket claim about 'captures' has to become a claim about the player/host captures — which is the README owner's to make once. OWNER: whoever owns docs/evidence/screenshots/README.md. SEVERITY: low — documentation only; no capture is wrong today, and every editor capture that exists demonstrably works without either mechanism.

title: The status bar renders no object or selection counts, though the bible, the spec and Task 4's own outcome all put counts on the left
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 10 (the parity capture's difference list, row 22), REPORTED to the controller rather than filed because Task 10 files no row, and VERIFIED BY THE CONTROLLER against the code before filing, because it is a claim about what the product does not do. Bible section 7.6 is normative and explicit: the status bar is '26px, mono, --faint, readouts only: object and selection counts on the left, save state and the live indicator on the right.' The spec's section 3.4 repeats it ('readouts only: counts, save state, live indicator'), bible section 7's own diagram prints `status bar   counts ... saved - live`, and plan 2's Task 4 made it its first Outcome line - 'a 26px full-width strip, mono, carrying counts on the left' - and named `hosts.status` as 'the span `editor-main` writes counts and messages into'. THE PRODUCT RENDERS NO COUNT. The footer is `<footer id="status">` (shell-layout.tsx:783) holding the status host span, DiagnosticMessage, SaveState and PublishIndicator, and EVERY write into that span is a message: editor-main.ts:115, :123, :185, :245, :256, :271, :274, :277, :343, :355, :357, :391 and :400 - thirteen of them, ending at 'Fabric editor ready'. `git log --oneline -S 'objects selected' --all` returns no code commit at all, only a docs/plans commit and Task 10's own difference table. So the span has never carried a count; the capture shows the left reading as 'Fabric editor ready' and the mockup shows '52 objects   0 selected'. THE SELECTION HALF IS ALREADY COMPUTED AND UNUSED AS A READING: EditorShellSnapshot.selectedCount is real (bridge.ts:29, computed at :159 as 1 or the ActiveSelection's length), and its production consumers are the dock's arrange eligibility via memberCount (bridge.ts:179) and an effect dependency at shell-layout.tsx:407 - and neither renders it as a reading. The object count is not in the snapshot at all, so the fix is not purely presentational. A CONTROLLER ERROR IS PART OF THIS ROW, recorded because it is why the gap survived review: in Task 4's fix round I ruled that `hosts.status` was 'the counts span' - a description inherited from the brief and repeated without checking - and it is not; the comment that ruling corrected was still right for the reason it gave, but the description under it was false, and five rounds of review plus the whole-branch pass never looked at whether anything wrote counts into it. OWNER: whoever owns the status bar next (plan 2 closes with this row; the strip itself is plan 2's surface). It needs a design decision first: what the object count reads, where it comes from (the bridge exposes selection but not the scene's object total), and whether the diagnostic keeps the same span or yields to the counts. SEVERITY: medium - the bible's only stated content for the left half of the status bar is missing, and Task 4's review passed a strip whose mandated content does not exist. CORRECTED 2026-10-09 by plan 2's final whole-branch review, which found this row's consumer claim incomplete: shell-layout.tsx:407 also lists selection.selectedCount as an effect dependency. The conclusion is unchanged - nothing renders the count.

title: The shell's four body regions are inset 8px and rounded at an off-scale 12px radius, where the bible's diagram draws them flush and section 3 has no 12px step
detail: FOUND BY plan 2 Task 10 (difference list row 19), REPORTED to the controller rather than filed, and VERIFIED BY THE CONTROLLER before filing - both halves. (1) THE INSET: `.editor-shell-body` is `gap: 8px` at editor-shell.css:761 and `padding: 8px` at :764, so rail, pane, stage and inspector float as separated cards, where bible section 7's diagram draws the four regions abutting, separated by `|` characters in one box. Nothing in the bible states the inset, so this is a layout decision no document owns either way. (2) THE RADIUS, which is the sharper half because the bible has a closed table for it: `border-radius: 12px` at editor-shell.css:784 (.editor-shell-rail), :833 (.editor-shell-inspector), :1016 (.vigilia-dialog), :1064 (.editor-shell-dialog) and :1601 (.editor-shell-stage), against section 3's scale - --radius-sm 4, --radius-md 6, --radius-lg 8, --radius-xl 10 - which this very file declares at :301-302. There is no 12px step, so all five values are off-scale, and they are on the surfaces plan 2 built (rail, inspector, stage) as well as the two dialogs. WHY IT SURVIVED EVERY GATE: editor-shell.css is DELIBERATELY UNGATED - plan 2's Task 8 recorded it as a before-state for plan 3 rather than adding it to scripts/design-tokens.gated.json - so the one instrument that reads spacing and radius values never opens this file, and the file is also outside the design-language fixture (the fixture mounts the control set over the built stylesheet, not the shell). Same family as vg-227 (the rail's 34px slot): an off-scale value that no mechanism watches, on a surface whose task is closed. OWNER: first a design decision - whether the bible gains a 12px step for the shell's own regions, or the regions move to --radius-xl (10) or --radius-lg (8); separately, whether the body insets at all or becomes flush per section 7's diagram. Then whoever owns editor-shell.css. SEVERITY: low - nothing breaks and nothing is unreachable; the finding is that the shell's largest layout fact and five radius values are owned by no document and watched by no gate. CORRECTED 2026-10-09 by plan 2's final whole-branch review, which found this row's line citation off by four: the `gap` is at :761 and the `padding` at :764, both inside the same .editor-shell-body rule, not at :757. The five 12px radii and the --radius-* citations were already exact, and the conclusion is unchanged. UPDATE 2026-10-10, THE USER'S RULING, which closes this row's open question: the mockup is NOT replaced — in the user's words, "Do not replace the mockup. Even the setting panel you just built looks nothing like it. Goddamn it why is it so hard to stay on target when we already have a clear visual mockup?" So the alternative this row left open is settled in favour of the product work: the drawing stays the target and the shipped surface is pulled to it, which makes the 8px inset and the four literal 12px radii a decided defect to fix rather than a difference to adjudicate. Scheduled by the mockup-parity plan this ruling requires, not by this row.

title: A globals edit reaches six owners on the palette path and three on the type path, so a renamed type preset leaves the inspector printing the old name
detail: FOUND by a read-only architecture survey the user asked for ('does any domain manager need clean-up — same domain spread across a few managers, a domain under another owner that should be its own'), run on 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. VERIFIED BY ME from source, not taken from the survey. There is no owner for 'a globals edit must reach every consumer': editor-session.ts decides the receiver list inline, once per setter, and the lists disagree. #setPalette (editor-session.ts:1145-1158) calls shell.setGlobals, #runtime.setGlobals, charts.setGlobals, #newObjects.setGlobals, #artboard.setGlobals and #selection.setGlobals — SIX owners plus two renders. #setTypes (:1187-1194) calls three: shell, #runtime, #newObjects. #deleteType (:1219-1235) calls two — it omits #runtime as well. The consequence is behavioural: the inspector reads type-preset names and resolutions out of context.globals (per-kind-column.ts:545-546 and :607-608 call nameOfRef/resolveTypePreset on it), and selection-inspector/index.ts:524 is the only thing that updates that value. Because #setTypes never calls it, renaming a type preset leaves Spends printing the OLD name until an unrelated object:modified or selection event re-renders, which index.ts:491-517 lists as the only triggers. The source also asserts the wrong thing in prose: live-runtime.ts:103-108 says 'the session hands new globals to six owners (editor-session.ts:1041-1046)', true on one path of three, and the lines it cites now fall inside #release. NOT MEASURED: whether the missing charts.setGlobals and #artboard.setGlobals on the type path have their own visible staleness — I verified the inspector's only. SHAPE PRECEDENT: vg-058 (verified) is the same failure one instance smaller. OWNER: unassigned; the fix is one 'globals changed' fan-out the session owns, not four lists. SEVERITY: medium — a stale label that misreports what the document says.

title: The authored text box has three writers and one stores the scaled width that the shared writer's own comment says would grow the box on every pass
detail: FOUND by a read-only architecture survey the user asked for ('does any domain manager need clean-up — same domain spread across a few managers, a domain under another owner that should be its own'), run on 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. VERIFIED BY ME by reading both writers. authored-box.ts:196-197 documents writeAuthoredBoxDimension as 'The single write every geometry surface shares'. It is not single: three writers touch vigiliaText.box — the shared helper (called from controls-manager/index.ts:255), selection-inspector/index.ts:70-95 writeAuthoredBox (inline, both dimensions), and text-manager/index.ts:79-92 adoptResizedBox (inline, width). The three disagree about units, and the source says which is right: authored-box.ts:70-74 'vigiliaText.box is scene units; Fabric's width is the same box before scaleX', and writeAuthoredBoxDimension seeds with the UNSCALED object.width/object.height under a comment (:216) reading 'Seeding with the scaled value would grow the box on every pass'. text-manager/index.ts:90 does exactly that — width: target.width * scaleX. Because boxFrom (authored-box.ts:42-62) multiplies by scaleX on read, storing the scaled value makes the read-back scaleX squared for a scaled object. The inline writers also skip the helper's refusals: the value < 1 / non-finite guard (:203) and the sibling-dimension seeding (:209-223) that exists so an object never loses its width. NOT ESTABLISHED: reachability — the survey could not trace whether scaleX can be non-1 when adoptResizedBox runs, since the width guard puts object.width back before object:resizing reports and whether it resets scaleX is untraced. What would settle it: one browser check, scale a text object, drag a side handle, compare vigiliaText.box.width against width * scaleX. UNTIL THAT RUNS THIS IS A CONTRADICTION IN SOURCE, NOT A MEASURED DEFECT. selection-inspector/index.ts is a file another agent is mid-task on, so that writer may be moving. NEAR ROWS: vg-057 (verified, the half-box), vg-109, vg-112 — none names the three writers. OWNER: scene-fabric/src/authored-box.ts, which already claims the job and should hold the only writer. SEVERITY: medium if reachable, low if the guard makes it unreachable — hence the one check first.

title: Renaming an object is written in two places, they refuse differently, and the validity guard lives in a module the ownership map does not name
detail: FOUND by a read-only architecture survey the user asked for ('does any domain manager need clean-up — same domain spread across a few managers, a domain under another owner that should be its own'), run on 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. Verified from source. The validity RULE has one owner and is shared correctly — renderer-core/src/theme/object-name.ts:33 isObjectName — but that module has NO row in ownership.md, and by the map's own preamble a module owning a concept while appearing nowhere in the map is invisible, so nothing warns a reader not to decide it elsewhere. The two writers of the FACT disagree on the refusal path: editor-shell/bridge.ts:323-324 (layer-row rename) returns silently at :329, while selection-inspector/appearance.ts:339 reports through errorManager.warn('controls', uiCopy.inspectorFields.invalidName) at :319-325. They notify differently too: bridge fires nothing and relies on the session subscription (bridge.ts:148), while appearance.ts:345-350 fires object:modified itself. So typing a refused name has two outcomes depending on which surface it was typed in — one author action, two behaviours. NOT ESTABLISHED: neither writer was traced past the refusal branch. OWNER: unassigned; the name write belongs with the object's identity, and both surfaces should call it. SEVERITY: low — the name is refused either way, and the divergence is in what the author is told.

title: The save's picture fallback is written twice: #save spells the expression inline while #writeLibrary calls #picture

title: The snap manager implements one acquire-hold-plan-verify protocol twice, split movement-versus-scale — the duplicated axis — rather than by the sub-domains that are genuinely separate
detail: FOUND by a read-only architecture survey the user asked for ('does any domain manager need clean-up — same domain spread across a few managers, a domain under another owner that should be its own'), run on 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. The largest structural finding of the set, and the answer to the user's companion worry that several files have crossed the 500-line signal. snap-manager/ is ~8,300 non-test lines across eight files and roughly 4,900 of them are ONE concept implemented twice, which the guards confirm as well as the shapes: the movement family's assertMovementHoldState/assertRawIntentMatchesBaseline (movement-snapping-resolver.ts:313-314) and assertAxisHold (:1315-1316) are mirrored by the scale family's checks in scaling/scale-projection.ts:95,117,156,186,187 and scaling/scale-snapping-runtime.ts:84-229. The parallel-for-parallel evidence: identical threshold records with identical values (movement-snapping-resolver.ts:81-87 with MOVEMENT_SNAP_VERIFICATION_EPSILON = 0.1 at :203 versus scaling/scale-snapping-resolver.ts:88-94 with SCALE_SNAP_VERIFICATION_EPSILON = 0.1 at :243); parallel frozen holds (FREE_MOVEMENT_HOLD_STATE :240 / FREE_SCALE_HOLD_STATE :265); runtimes exposing the same five-method protocol (movement-snapping-runtime.ts:75-190 startSession/getDuplicateStep/resolveMovementPlan/verifyMovementPlan/finishSession versus scaling/scale-snapping-runtime.ts:84-229 the same shape with resolveScalePlan/refineScalePlan/verifyScalePlan); and parallel candidate builders (movement-snap-candidates.ts:23-76 versus scaling/scale-snap-candidates.ts). GENUINELY SEPARATE and not the duplicated part: spacing (spacing.ts at 1302 lines plus spacing-chains.ts, spacing-patterns.ts, movement-spacing-correction.ts, movement-spacing-verification.ts) and pointer-to-multiplier projection (scaling/rectangular-scale-gesture-projection.ts at 985, scale-projection.ts at 726). WHY IT IS A MANAGER QUESTION: the axis the module is split on — movement versus scale — is the axis that duplicated, while the sub-domains that are actually distinct are not the split; that is why the family carries five files over 700 lines and three over 1,300. NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the two protocols fold into one parameterised by axis without disturbing spacing and projection, which is the design question. The map's footer already names 'advanced snapping' as a review-only legacy candidate, so this is a candidate for a spec rather than a task. OWNER: unassigned. SEVERITY: low today (it works and is tested), high as the reason the editor's largest module family is the largest.

title: The map gives the artboard-to-viewport transform to renderer-core, but no editor module calls it — the camera re-implements contain and centring itself
detail: FOUND by a read-only architecture survey the user asked for ('does any domain manager need clean-up — same domain spread across a few managers, a domain under another owner that should be its own'), run on 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. Nothing in the editor calls it: the only callers are renderer-core/src/scene/mount.ts:83 and scene-fabric/src/scene.ts:116, i.e. the plan and player path. Meanwhile the editor's camera re-implements the rule, unguarded: viewport-manager/index.ts fitScaleFor (:209-214) re-derives contain as Math.min(box.width / board.width, box.height / board.height) clamped to MIN_ZOOM/MAX_ZOOM (:11-12), and fitTransformIn (:224-237) re-derives the centring. So the map's Editor table has a row whose owner the editor never uses, and the editor's version of that invariant has no single owner and none of the guard's refusals. NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the editor's fit is deliberately a different rule (fit to the display's screen rather than the host — the comment at :230-233 says exactly that) or a copy that drifted; if it is deliberate it needs its own row and its own guard, and if it is a copy the two should meet. OWNER: whoever owns the map, plus viewport-manager. SEVERITY: medium — the contain rule is an invariant and only one of its two copies is guarded.

title: The `locked` predicate has no owner: the lock manager owns writing the flag but not testing it, so eight modules spell the test themselves
detail: FOUND by the reverse-direction read the user asked for after the manager-ownership survey ('does any manager turn out to be too small or narrow a concept to stand on its own and should be folded into another?'), run 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. The answer to the question as put is no — every manager checked owns at least one decision nobody else owns — and these two rows are what the read actually found: the inverse defect, a shared fact that no module owns and every consumer re-spells. THE FACT. `object.get("locked")` is read in 11 non-test places across 8 modules: object-lock-manager/index.ts:40 (its private `isLocked`) and :81 (the one write); deletion-manager/index.ts:15 (`deletable`, `!== true`); clipboard-manager/index.ts:310 and :338 (`=== true`, twice inline); controls-manager/index.ts:82 and :157 (`!== true`, twice inline); indicator-manager/index.ts:93; editor-shell/bridge.ts:165; selection-inspector/index.ts:395; selection-inspector/per-kind-column.ts:634; selection-inspector/view.ts:466. By the map's own instrument — find the code that would reject a wrong value for a concept and ask whether it lives in the module the map names — this guard lives in eight modules and the map names none of them for it. object-lock-manager owns the flag's derivation from Fabric's transform flags (TRANSFORM_LOCKED/TRANSFORM_FREE, `hasControls` load-bearing) and the re-derivation on history load, but its predicate is private, so every other reader re-derives the vocabulary. WHY IT MATTERS. The polarity is not even consistent — `=== true` in five places, `!== true` in three — which is invisible today because both are falsy-safe, and stops being invisible the moment a third lock state exists (a partial lock, a group whose members differ). Then it is eight edit sites the map cannot list. This is the map's stated failure exactly: 're-spelling the set, or a subset of it, somewhere else is a second owner, and it fails quietly.' NOT ESTABLISHED: which module should own the predicate. object-lock-manager is the natural candidate but may sit above some of its readers in the import graph, in which case the fact belongs lower down (the same question vg-248 raises) — that ordering is the design decision the row waits on. NOT CLAIMED: that any current reader is wrong; all eleven agree on today's two states. OWNER: whoever owns the ownership map and the lock manager.

title: The fact 'which collection holds this object' is spelled in four modules with three different return contracts, and its ActiveSelection companion in four more
detail: FOUND by the reverse-direction read the user asked for after the manager-ownership survey ('does any manager turn out to be too small or narrow a concept to stand on its own and should be folded into another?'), run 2026-10-09 with docs/architecture/ownership.md as the yardstick. The answer to the question as put is no — every manager checked owns at least one decision nobody else owns — and these two rows are what the read actually found: the inverse defect, a shared fact that no module owns and every consumer re-spells. THE FACT. `parent instanceof Group` appears at four sites with three contracts: layer-manager/index.ts:24 `ownerOf` returning `Canvas | Group` (falling back to the canvas); deletion-manager/index.ts:25 returning `Canvas | Group | undefined` (its caller writes `ownerOf(object) ?? canvas`); editor-shell/layer-tree.ts:466 returning `Group | undefined`; and editor-shell/bridge.ts:278, which uses the same test to pick a child rather than a holder. Its companion — 'an ActiveSelection lives outside `_objects`, so move its members' — is spelled four times too: layer-manager/index.ts:30 (a named `targetsOf`), deletion-manager/index.ts:37 (inline), canvas-nudge.ts:46 (inline), history-manager/index.ts:114 (inline). deletion-manager's `ownerOf` is a near-copy of layer-manager's with a different signature, and its inline targets expression is layer-manager's named function retyped; the two modules do not import one another. WHY IT MATTERS. The comments on those functions record learned Fabric traps, not style: layer-manager/index.ts:18-22 ('a move issued on the canvas to a group child *inserts* it into the root and leaves it in both arrays — painted and serialised twice') and deletion-manager/index.ts:18-22 ('`Collection.remove` searches only its own `_objects` and returns an empty removal for anything else'). A trap documented in four places is a trap that gets fixed in one of them. The divergent signatures are the mechanism: a caller that forgets `?? canvas` silently gets `undefined` where the other three implementations would have handed it the canvas. NOTE. This is the same shape as vg-240 (one protocol implemented twice) at the helper scale, and it is why deletion-manager reads as a fold candidate — it is not too small, it shares a fact with layer-manager and neither owns it. NOT ESTABLISHED: which module should own it. The fact is pure Fabric knowledge rather than editor policy, so scene-fabric (which already carries shared Fabric facts, e.g. authored-box.ts) is a candidate alongside layer-manager. OWNER: whoever owns the map, with the layer and deletion managers.

title: A text run has no identity in the persisted model, so the inspector's row keys must come from content — an edit or a same-shape middle removal changes the key and costs the row its caret
detail: FOUND WHILE EXECUTING PLAN 3, TASK 3, during its fix loop. The run editor keys each row by a derived identity because `vigiliaText.runs` is a plain array with no per-run id. Two attempts were made and each trades one failure for another, which is the evidence that the model is the cause rather than the key. (1) Positional index keys: the row survives an edit, but removing a MIDDLE run shifts every later index, so React reconciles a row holding a draft onto the next run's data — the draft is displayed against the wrong run and the next blur can commit it there (filed as M1 in the task review). (2) Content-derived identity `` `literal:${typePreset}\u0000${text}` ``: a middle removal is then safe, because survivors keep their keys, but `ControlText` commits on ENTER (`components/ui/control-text.tsx:74`), so committing a typed reading changes the key, remounts the row, destroys the focused input and drops focus to `document.body` (N1). The shipped fix excludes the mutable TEXT from the identity, which removes the Enter failure and leaves a residual, recorded in `runs.tsx` rather than hidden: two literal runs sharing a type preset can still shift on a middle removal, and changing a run's preset or its source binding still remounts that row. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS TASK. Task 3a's brief requires it to preserve 'repeat-row identity' for chart series rows, which is the same problem over the same kind of array, so it will be met again before the plan closes. PRECEDENT, NOT A GUESS. The same class was already found and fixed once: vg-044 (archived, verified) — 'A chart's series colours and its bindings are coupled by index, so removing a middle binding shifts the colours' — and its fix was NOT an id. It reconciles at mutation time, carrying each surviving series' own paint through the removal before the array-length repair runs. So the cheap path here is probably the same shape: carry the surviving rows' state through the removal (or hold drafts outside the row), rather than adding a persisted id. NOT ESTABLISHED: whether reconciliation is sufficient for the caret case, since a lost draft and a misplaced draft are different harms, or whether the model should simply gain a per-run id — that is a persisted-schema decision (existing documents hold runs without one) and is not a task-level call. NOT CLAIMED: that the shipped fix is wrong; it is the best of the three shapes available without a model change, and its residual is disclosed in code and in the task report. OWNER: whoever owns the persisted text-run model with whoever owns the inspector's row rendering.

title: The conversion to React field views left tests silently vacuous — a selector that no longer matches and a raw change event that no longer commits both still pass, so two instances were known and one is still live (the stale-opacity case; the Position accessible-name audit is fixed at 7841ec2d) and nothing detects a third
detail: FOUND WHILE EXECUTING PLAN 3, TASK 4. `index.dom.test.ts`'s 'refuses a stale opacity event rather than mutating the old selection' (base line 662) drives `[data-vigilia-opacity]` the pre-plan way — `input.value = "10"; input.dispatchEvent(new Event("change"))`. Task 3 converted Layer's opacity to a plan-1 `ControlNumber` (commit on blur, value held in React state), so the raw assignment is suppressed by React's value tracker and no commit is attempted. The case still passes because both its assertions — `rect.opacity` stays 0.5 and `saveState` is not called — are equally true when nothing was committed. WHY IT MATTERS. Task 4's brief names this test as the control for Step 2's requirement that the stale-draft refusal survives the conversion, so the plan believes a refusal it cannot fail is covered. The refusal does exist one layer down: `view.ts`'s `editRefusal` compares the revision the view was projected from with the live `targetRevision` and returns "stale", and `view.test.ts`'s 'reports a stale draft ahead of the lock it would also fail' proves that unit. What is missing is a DOM-level proof, and the architecture makes one hard to write deliberately: a republish keys each row by `${revision}:${fieldId}`, so a control bound to a superseded object is unmounted and can deliver no event. NOT ESTABLISHED: whether a DOM proof is worth having, or whether the `editRefusal` unit case plus the four 'a draft and the object it describes' cases are the whole contract. This row is the same class as Task 3's leftovers: a case that reads green because the markup it drives moved. OWNER: whoever owns the inspector's test suite, alongside Task 7's locator sweep. SECOND INSTANCE, FOUND IN THE SAME PLAN, TASK 4 TASK REVIEW (2026-10-09, agent a6d8ea92dc02ac4bf). panel.dom.test.ts:550 ("gives every field on a %s an accessible name") selects ".vigilia-field > input, .vigilia-field > select, .vigilia-field > textarea, .vigilia-field-row input". The converted fields render through plan 1 control set, which emits data-vigilia-* hooks and Tailwind classes and no .vigilia-field at all, so as Position converted, the selector narrowed to fewer and fewer controls while the case kept passing. Its own guard is what let that happen silently: expect(controls.length).toBeGreaterThan(0) cannot tell "every field" from "one field". An accessible-name assertion that has narrowed is worse than a missing one, because the coverage it appears to give is counted. WHY ONE ROW AND NOT TWO. Both instances are the same problem, and the repair is the same job: a test that predates the conversion has to be re-pointed at what the converted surface actually emits. Filing them separately would hide that the class is at least twice as large as either sighting, and the real fix is a sweep rather than two patches. WHAT A SWEEP HAS TO DECIDE. Whether each re-pointed case is still needed at all: src/web/packages/editor/src/accessible-names.dom.test.ts (added by plan 3 task 3) audits accessibility for a FIXED list of mounted panels. It is NOT a duplicate of the Position case and must not be used to justify deleting it: that audit mounts the inspector on two specific selections (its own words at :224-234, the richest being a text object with a run bound to a clock), while panel.dom.test.ts case is it.each(SHAPES) and sweeps every shape kind, which the audit does not. The audit is explicit that its panel list IS its coverage and that a green run there must not be read as the editor being clean. So the repair is to re-point the per-shape case at what the converted surface emits and to STRENGTHEN its controls.length > 0 guard, not to delete it. PATH CORRECTED 2026-10-09: an earlier revision of this row said editor-shell/, which is wrong; the file is at the package root. That is a judgement per case, which is why this is a row and not a one-line fix. NOT ESTABLISHED: how many instances exist. Two were found by two different reviews reading different files, which is evidence of a class rather than a count. A sweep should look for every test whose selector or event predates the control set, in the selection-inspector and anywhere else a plan-3 task has converted a surface. RECORD HARDENED 2026-10-09 by plan 3's final whole-branch review, which found the count reading high: the Position accessible-name instance is FIXED at HEAD (7841ec2d, the audit's skip rule), so only the stale-opacity case is still live. Re-measured at the controller's hand: index.dom.test.ts:713-724 still drives [data-vigilia-opacity] with `opacity.value = "10"; dispatchEvent(new Event("change"))`, and that element is now a SLIDER by plan 3 Task 9's fix, so a raw change can no longer reach a commit path at all - the conversion made the remaining instance more vacuous rather than less, and its two assertions (opacity stays 0.5, saveState not called) are both true when nothing was attempted. The detection gap the title names is unchanged and still open.

title: isTextEntryTarget counts a range input as a text-entry target, so every shortcut the manager owns is swallowed while a slider has focus
detail: FOUND WHILE EXECUTING PLAN 3, TASK 7 (fix round 1, commit 4bf29bf6), which added it as a `Discovered, not fixed:` trailer. `isTextEntryTarget` (src/web/packages/editor/src/shortcut-manager/index.ts:192-213) returns true for any HTMLInputElement whose type is not in a small exclusion set - button, checkbox, color, file, image, radio, reset, submit (:202-211). `range` is not in that set, so a focused input[type=range] is treated as a text-entry target, the handler at :143-147 sets `deferred`, and the manager returns before preventDefault() and before the bound handler. CONSEQUENCE, AND IT IS WIDER THAN THE TRAILER AND THE COMMIT MESSAGE SAY: both name Ctrl+Z (undo swallowed while a slider has focus), but the predicate gates EVERY action the shortcut table binds, so Delete, Escape and the rest are swallowed too. The controller verified the cause at source rather than taking the trailer's word for it. WHY THE FIX IS NOT JUST ADDING range TO THE SET: the same predicate guards the bare-key canvas listeners (camera keys), so a range was presumably left in deliberately - an unmodified arrow on a focused slider must move the slider, not the camera. Ctrl+Z is a modifier chord with no native meaning on a range, so it should reach the manager while an unmodified arrow should not. That makes the repair a decision about which keys a non-text control still defers, not a one-line set edit. AUTHOR-FACING AND REACHABLE: click the slider, press Ctrl+Z, nothing happens. BLAST RADIUS: every ControlSlider the plan-1 control set renders, which after this plan is polygon sides, the shape sweep pair and glass blur. NOT FIXED HERE because the owner is shortcut-manager and the task that found it is the inspector, and the correct behaviour is a ruling rather than a patch.

title: A slider in the selection column gives no live preview while dragging, so the value only moves on release
detail: FOUND WHILE REVIEWING PLAN 3 TASK 9 (the parity capture), in the built editor at 1ab06ad2, by the task reviewer and verified at source by the controller while filing. MEASURED: with the Layer Opacity slider focused, a pointer drag to roughly 50% and then 25% left aria-valuenow AND the well reading 99 throughout, and the value jumped to 26 only on mouse-up - so an author dragging a bounded number sees nothing change until they let go. CAUSE, read rather than guessed: selection-inspector/column.tsx:183-192 renders ControlSlider with onCommit and no onPreview, although the control supports a preview callback (components/ui/control-slider.tsx:30 and :112, described in its own docblock at :17) and components/ui/control.dom.test.tsx:659-676 exercises it. The field funnel has no preview half to call: SelectionEdits exposes only commit, where the sibling CropEdits (selection-inspector/view.ts:269-274) has begin/setAspect/apply/cancel. NOT A BIBLE VIOLATION, which is why this is filed rather than fixed: design-language.md section 5 says a slider MAY preview through the existing imperative write funnel, so preview is permitted and not required, and release committing one changed value is satisfied as it stands. SHARED, NOT INTRODUCED HERE: the same field renderer draws the glass blur and panel radius sliders, so every slider in the column behaves this way and the behaviour predates plan 3's Task 9. WHY IT NEEDS A RULING RATHER THAN A PATCH: giving sliders a preview means adding a preview/cancel path to the field funnel and deciding how a preview that writes nothing interacts with the one-undo-boundary rule the same section states, across the control set, the funnel and the history boundary - a design decision with more than one owner, not a missing prop.

title: selection-inspector/index.ts grew from 540 to 822 lines, past the plan's own holds-or-shrinks constraint

title: writeOpacity is the selection column's sole 0-100 enforcement and has no test
detail: FOUND BY PLAN 3'S FINAL WHOLE-BRANCH REVIEW (2026-10-09) as the sharpest residual of the close, and descended from Ruling AH in the plan's ledger. selection-inspector/index.ts:469-482 refuses a value outside 0-100 and warns; plan 3 Task 9 converted the Layer Opacity field from a text box to a slider (appearance.ts opacityField, control 'slider', min 0, max 100, integer true), which DELETED the only route by which an author could produce an out-of-range value - so the two text-box tests that drove the refusal had nothing left to drive and were replaced by a slider test that exercises the control's own bound. NO CONTRIVED ROUTE EXISTS, checked rather than assumed: Base UI clamps inside handleInputChange -> getSliderValue (SliderRoot.mjs:177-190) before onValueCommitted fires, SelectionInspector exposes no seam (index.ts:67-75 - root, render, setGlobals, setLocale only), writeOpacity is not exported, and editRefusal can never produce 'invalid' for this field because view.ts:380 types the opacity kind as 'number'. Fixing it means either a public test seam added for a test's sake or a contrived injection that would prove Base UI's clamping rather than this guard.
